student.question: Is a healthcare intervention worth its cost?
student.description: Explore how healthcare systems decide whether treatments, technologies and interventions provide enough value to justify their costs.
student.centralQuestion: How should limited healthcare resources be used?
student.overview: Healthcare systems constantly face difficult choices. A treatment may save lives but cost hundreds of thousands of euros. Economic evaluation helps decision-makers compare costs, outcomes and uncertainty in a systematic way.
student.typicalProblem: A new therapy can significantly improve survival, but its cost is extremely high. How should we measure its long-term benefits? Which costs should count? How much should the healthcare system be willing to pay?
fit: You are interested in pharmaceuticals, HTA or market access.
You like asking whether an intervention provides enough value for its cost.
You enjoy structured decision-making under uncertainty.

student.question: Does a health policy actually work, and for whom?
student.description: Use economics, econometrics and real-world evidence to understand how health policies influence costs, access, behaviour, equity and health outcomes.
student.centralQuestion: How can we know whether a healthcare policy actually improves society?
student.overview: Healthcare policies affect prices, behaviour, access, inequality, spending and health outcomes. This track combines economic theory with quantitative analysis to understand these effects and support better policy decisions.
student.typicalProblem: A government wants to cap medicine prices. Will the policy reduce spending? Could it affect innovation or medicine availability? Will the effects be equal across different groups?
fit: You enjoy statistics and empirical research.
You are interested in government and healthcare policy.
You want to understand whether policies cause measurable change.
You like combining economics with real-world data.

student.question: How do we make healthcare organisations work better?
student.description: Explore how healthcare organisations can lead people, manage resources, respond to change and deliver better care in complex environments.
student.centralQuestion: How do you lead a healthcare organisation through complexity and change?
student.overview: Hospitals and healthcare organisations constantly balance quality, people, finances, regulation, innovation and limited resources. This track looks at healthcare from the perspective of the organisation and the people who lead it.
student.typicalProblem: A hospital faces staff shortages, rising admissions and financial pressure while considering a major digital-health investment. How should leadership balance innovation, finances, staff support and patient care?
fit: You are interested in leadership and management.
You can imagine working with hospitals, providers or healthcare companies.
You like combining people, strategy, finance and innovation.

student.question: How can we improve the health of entire populations?
student.description: Understand the wider social, economic and environmental drivers of health and learn how evidence-based interventions can improve outcomes across communities.
student.centralQuestion: How can we improve health before people ever reach the hospital?
student.overview: Health outcomes are shaped by far more than medical treatment. Income, environment, behaviour, access, education and social conditions all matter. This track looks at how health systems and communities can design interventions that improve outcomes at scale.
student.typicalProblem: A low-income community has high rates of diabetes, hypertension and obesity. Medical treatment alone has not solved the problem. Which social, environmental and healthcare factors drive these outcomes, and what population-level intervention could change them?
fit: You care about prevention and inequalities.
You enjoy public or global health.
You want to understand health at community and system level.
You are interested in epidemiology, environment and social determinants of health.

texts.careerHeading: Your track does not define your career
texts.careerText: The tracks create different areas of emphasis, but EU-HEM remains an interdisciplinary degree. Alumni across tracks work in consulting, pharmaceutical and biotech companies, research, government, healthcare providers, international organisations and technology-related roles. Your internships, thesis, background and later experience also shape where you go next.

faq.a: No. The submitted choice is final.

faq.q: Does my track determine my thesis university?
faq.a: You write your thesis at one of the two universities of your track.

faq.q: Does choosing one track limit me to one industry?
faq.a: No. Career sectors overlap significantly across tracks.

It depends on what you mean by quantitative, and on your electives. From the course lists: EEH requires modelling courses (Advanced Health Economic Modelling, Modeling in Economic Evaluation II) and Research Design. E&P requires Applied Micro Econometrics. PHM requires Analysis and Epidemiology. MHI requires Economic Evaluation and Qualitative Research Methods, and offers Applied Micro Econometrics and data courses as Semester 2 electives.

faq.q: Is one track better for a PhD?
faq.a: Research and PhD paths appear among the common sectors of several tracks. What matters is the research questions and methods that interest you.

faq.q: Should I choose based on cities?
faq.a: City matters, but academic content and professional interests should come first.
